newsitem.title: USA: Albright readies new appointments at State.
newsitem.headline: Albright readies new appointments at State.

text.p: With Senate confirmation behind her, Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright was readying a roster of top advisers that include professionals who will bring experience and depth to her team, U.S. officials said on Wednesday.
Albright, after unanimous Senate approval, was to be sworn in as the first woman secretary of state on Thursday.

Officials said she has tapped Thomas Pickering, former U.S. ambassador to Russia and one of the most experienced U.S. diplomats, for the number three post as undersecretary of state for political affairs, replacing Peter Tarnoff.
Also, Stuart Eizenstat, the Commerce Department's undersecretary for international trade, will be undersecretary of state for economic affairs, succeeding Joan Spero.
"The objective is the strongest possible team," one administration official told Reuters.

Pickering, United Nations ambassador under former President George Bush and then-Secretary of State James Baker, has a long and distinguished career. His appointment heartened members of America's career foreign service.

Although Albright has made her career in international relations and is well-versed on most issues, she approached the subject mostly as a politician, serving as adviser to former Senator Edmund Muskie and unsuccessful Democratic presidential candidates Walter Mondale and Mike Dukakis. Her inner circle of aides includes many political appointees.

Eizenstat, domestic policy adviser for President Jimmy Carter, bailed President Bill Clinton out of a serious jam last year. He led the effort to persuade Europe to take stronger action on human rights in Cuba, allowing Clinton to waive a section of the anti-Castro Helms-Burton law that had set Washington on a collision course with its allies.

The State Department hailed the smooth transition to Albright from predecessor Warren Christopher. But one official told Reuters: "Albright's going to be changing a lot of people and it's not quite as friendly as one might think."
Many other appointments are decided or in the works:
-- Undersecretary of State for Global Affairs Tim Wirth and Agency for International Development Administrator Brian Atwood are expected to stay in those jobs

-- As previously announced, Strobe Talbott remains deputy secretary, the number two post. But speculation is he may leave in a few months, possibly to head the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, with Pickering moving up to deputy
-- Robert Gelbard, assistant secretary for international narcotics, is being discussed for undersecretary of state for arms control and international security affairs.

-- Elaine Shocas, chief of staff when Albright was U.N. envoy, will remain her chief of staff, while James Rubin, her spokesman, is expected to be assistant secretary of state for public affairs. Both are political appointees.

-- Stanley Roth, former National Security Council official, is due to be assistant secretary of state for East Asia and Pacific Affairs, replacing Winston Lord, while Mark Grossman, U.S. envoy to Turkey, is expected to be assistant secretary for European Affairs, replacing John Kornblum.

-- Kornblum is expected to be named ambassador to Germany while James Collins, who handles Russia and other ex-Soviet states at the State Department, is said to be the leading candidate to replace Pickering in Moscow.
-- Officials say there is a struggle for assistant secretary of state for Near East Affairs. Contenders include U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk among others.

-- Former congressman Howard Wolpe is expected to be named assistant secretary for African affairs, while National Security Council official Nancy Soderberg is to become a deputy to U.N. ambassador-designate Bill Richardson.

-- John Shattuck, human rights assistant secretary, is in line for U.S. envoy to the U.N. in Geneva. National Security Council Africa expert Susan Rice is said to be in line to replace Shattuck but some officials said she may be the new assistant secretary for intelligence and research.
